Period: From the return from exile through the New Testament period
Origin: The scribal class grew after the exile, when Israel lived under the written Law and needed trained men to copy, preserve, and teach it. Ezra is the model scribe, 'a ready scribe in the law of Moses.' By the first century, scribes were the professional students and teachers of Scripture, and in Luke's Gospel the experts among them are also called lawyers.
Beliefs: Scribes held Scripture as God's authoritative word and devoted themselves to its exact wording, interpretation, and application. Many shared Pharisaic convictions about the oral tradition, though scribes as a class were defined by their craft and learning rather than by one party's platform.
Practices: They copied and preserved the sacred texts, taught in synagogues and the Temple courts, drafted legal documents, and gave rulings on questions of the Law — what was lawful on the Sabbath, what counted as clean or unclean, how tithes and vows worked.
Role: Scribes were the educated class of Jewish society: respected teachers, legal advisers, and public figures. They sat on the Sanhedrin, debated in public, and were addressed as 'Rabbi.' Their learning gave them real authority with ordinary people, and real influence over how the Law was lived.
RelationshipToJesus: Jesus clashed with the scribes more than with any other group except the Pharisees. He affirmed their teaching seat yet condemned those who used the Law to burden people while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness. At the same time, some scribes were drawn to him, and the Gospels record scribes who questioned him honestly.
Scripture: Ezra 7:6; Nehemiah 8:1-8; Malachi 2:7; Matthew 23:1-3; Mark 12:38-40; Luke 11:45-52
Summary: The scribes were the trained teachers, copyists, and interpreters of God's Law — the scholars whose learning shaped how ordinary Jews heard and lived Scripture, and the group Jesus most often debated about what the Law truly requires.
